s: MSC Industrial Direct DEF 14A filed 11 Dec 2025, beneficial ownership table; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,154,540 Class A shares beneficially owned (3.9%) x $119.81 close 21 Aug 2026 = $258M; proxy footnote 4 shows no options in the total. Residence Brookville NY from his FEC contributor filings
did: Joined the family firm MSC Industrial in Melville in 1996 as an acquisition-integration manager, ran products and e-commerce, became COO in 2009 and CEO in January 2013, and moved the metalworking distributor from catalogue selling into vending machines, in-plant lockers and managed inventory, past $4B of sales.
why: MSC sells cutting tools where the customer's real cost is machine downtime, not unit price. Putting MSC-owned vending units and lockers inside the customer's plant made MSC the default requisition point, so reorders happened without a purchase decision and a cheaper rival had to physically displace hardware to win.
obst: From 2019 online price transparency destroyed the catalogue list-price model the company had run on for 60 years; customers priced-checked every SKU, sales and margin fell and the shares roughly halved, forcing him to rebuild profit through in-plant programmes rather than annual list increases.
turn: The January 2023 reclassification that collapsed MSC's dual-class structure, with the Jacobson and Gershwind family exchanging its Class B supervoting stock for 1.225 Class A shares each and turning a control block into ordinary liquid equity.

s: Global Industrial Company DEF 14A filed 22 Apr 2026, security ownership tables; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: Directors and officers as a group hold 24,682,193 shares (64.51%) x $39.45 close 21 Aug 2026 = $974M; the three founding brothers' individual figures overlap heavily through shared trusts, so the group is split in thirds. Residence from his FEC filings
did: With brothers Bruce and Robert turned the family's Port Washington mail-order supply business into Systemax, floated it in 1995, ran TigerDirect and CompUSA, then shut the computer-reselling arm between 2015 and 2017 and rebuilt the company as Global Industrial, a $1.4B MRO distributor.
why: Mail-order catalogues gave the family a customer list and a pick-and-pack network before either computers or industrial supplies mattered. When PC reselling died they kept the warehouses, the SKU data and the direct-marketing engine and simply repointed them at industrial goods, where gross margin is about 34% rather than 12%.
obst: Amazon and Newegg took the entire PC-reselling category the family had built its fortune on; between 2015 and 2017 they closed TigerDirect, sold the French and Dutch technology units and exited retail, writing off most of what had been the majority of group revenue.
turn: The 2017 sale of the European technology operations and the rename to Global Industrial, abandoning computers outright for industrial MRO.

s: Loar Holdings DEF 14A filed 14 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership table; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 4,371,005 shares beneficially owned (4.7%), including 284,000 exercisable options, x $75.00 close 21 Aug 2026 = $328M. Residence White Plains NY from his FEC contributor filings
did: A Trinidad-born accountant who had been CFO and then CEO of aircraft-brake maker K&F Industries, he co-founded Loar Group in White Plains in 2012 with Brett Milgrim and Abrams Capital, bought 18 small makers of sole-source certified aerospace parts, and listed Loar on the NYSE in April 2024 at $28.
why: Every part Loar owns is a certified sole-source component already flying. Getting an alternative approved costs an airframer more in engineering and FAA paperwork than the part is worth, so price is set by switching cost rather than competition, and the aftermarket half of revenue grows with the installed fleet for decades.
obst: The 2020 grounding hit a leveraged roll-up whose revenue was tied to flight hours; commercial aftermarket volumes collapsed and Loar had to hold its acquisition programme together on defence and niche general-aviation work until traffic returned in 2022.
turn: The April 2024 IPO, priced at $28 and closing about 60% higher on the first day, which repriced a privately assembled parts roll-up at a public aerospace multiple.

s: Napco Security Technologies DEF 14A filed 24 Oct 2025 and his Form 4 filings 2003-2026 on EDGAR; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,406,010 shares plus 108,000 exercisable options, about $55M at $38.09 on 21 Aug 2026, plus $282.0M of gross Form 4 sale proceeds 2003-2026 taxed at roughly 30% = about $252M
did: Joined Napco Security in Amityville at the start of the 1970s, became a director in 1972, chairman in 1981 and CEO in 1998, and converted a burglar-alarm hardware maker into a recurring-revenue business by selling StarLink cellular radios that carry alarm signals after copper phone lines were retired.
why: When carriers shut down analogue phone lines and then 2G and 3G, every installed alarm panel in America lost its path to the monitoring station. Napco made those panels, so it could sell a cellular radio plus a monthly airtime subscription into its own installed base, at recurring gross margins near 90%.
obst: Napco stayed a sub-$100M-revenue hardware maker for three decades against Honeywell's distribution, and its 2008 debt-funded purchase of Marks USA locking hardware left it overleveraged into the housing crash, forcing years of covenant renegotiation and offshore manufacturing moves to the Dominican Republic.
turn: The 2013 launch of StarLink cellular radios ahead of the AT&T 2G sunset, which turned a one-time hardware sale into a subscription and re-rated the stock from under $5 to above $40.

s: Kimco Realty DEF 14A filed 8 Apr 2026, beneficial ownership table; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 10,793,037 common shares and exchangeable OP and LTIP units x $24.02 close 21 Aug 2026 = $259M; age 95 in the Kimco proxy of 25 Mar 2024
did: A lawyer who in 1966 joined builder Martin Kimmel to buy strip shopping centres, naming the firm from their two surnames, took it public in November 1991 in the first modern REIT IPO, and built it into the largest US owner of open-air grocery-anchored centres before leaving the board in April 2025.
why: The 1991 IPO landed when the savings-and-loan collapse had shut off bank lending to real estate. Kimco could buy centres from forced sellers using public equity while every private rival was frozen out of debt, so it compounded acquisitions for a decade at capitalisation rates no leveraged buyer could match.
obst: Kimco's tenant base was the part of retail most exposed to bankruptcy; Kmart, Toys R Us, Bed Bath and Beyond and Rite Aid all failed as anchors, and the 2020 shutdown left rent collection near 70%, forcing the company to cut its dividend and re-lease space to grocers and off-price chains.
turn: The November 1991 IPO, which made Kimco the first modern equity REIT and gave a private partnership permanent public capital just as the property market bottomed.

s: Broadridge Financial Solutions DEF 14A filed 2 Oct 2025 and his Form 4 filings 2015-2025 on EDGAR; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 143,064 shares plus 558,149 exercisable options, about $61M at $182.18 on 21 Aug 2026, plus $146.8M of gross Form 4 sale proceeds 2015-2025 taxed at about 45% = roughly $142M. Residence Oyster Bay NY from his FEC filings
did: Joined Broadridge in Lake Success in 2010 as chief corporate development officer after running H&R Block's retail tax business, became COO in 2012 and CEO in January 2019, and moved the company from mailing paper proxies into digital shareholder communications, wealth platforms and blockchain repo settlement.
why: Broadridge distributes proxy and regulatory material for most US brokerage accounts under an NYSE-approved per-position fee schedule, so its revenue behaves like a levy on the equity market rather than a discretionary purchase. Shifting delivery from paper to digital cut its own cost while the fee stayed,
obst: The regulated proxy fee schedule is set by the NYSE and periodically attacked by brokers and issuers as a monopoly rent, and the 2017 acquisition of a securities-processing business plus the 2021 Itiviti deal loaded the balance sheet just as the SEC reopened the proxy-fee review.
turn: The 2020 shift of annual meetings and proxy delivery to fully digital during the pandemic, which permanently removed print and postage cost from a fee stream that did not fall.

s: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026 and his Form 4 filings 2020-2024 on EDGAR; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 52,213 shares, RSAs and 401k units plus 193,817 exercisable options valued at intrinsic worth against $834.04 on 21 Aug 2026, plus $57.6M of gross Form 4 sale proceeds 2020-2024 after tax; age 68 printed in the 2026 proxy
did: Joined Regeneron in Tarrytown in May 1999 as director of genomics, co-invented VelociGene and VelocImmune, the engineered-mouse platform that produces fully human antibodies, and rose to EVP Research and then co-chief scientific officer in January 2026; the platform produced Dupixent, Libtayo, Praluent and the Ebola cocktail.
why: Rival transgenic mice carried whole human antibody genes, so mouse signalling machinery could not mature them properly and affinity was weak. VelocImmune replaced only the variable regions and kept mouse constant regions, so the immune system worked normally, giving Regeneron better antibodies and a platform it could license out.
obst: Regeneron nearly failed twice around him, with the 1997 failure of its nerve-growth factor programme and the 2003 Axokine obesity trial collapse that cut the shares by two thirds, leaving the antibody platform to be funded out of partnership money rather than product revenue.
turn: The 2007 VelocImmune licences to AstraZeneca and Astellas, which paid Regeneron about $560M over six years for non-exclusive use of the mouse and financed its own pipeline without equity dilution.

s: Henry Schein DEF 14A filed 8 Apr 2026 and his Form 4 filings 2006-2026 on EDGAR; share price from stockanalysis.com, 21 Aug 2026
m: 455,675 shares plus options and unvested performance awards, about $58M at $88.50 on 21 Aug 2026, plus $110.8M of gross Form 4 sale proceeds 2006-2026 after tax; age 75 in the Apr 2025 proxy. Residence Northport NY from his FEC filings
did: A South African-born accountant who joined Henry Schein in 1980 as controller when it was a family drug distributor in Queens, became CEO in 1989, listed it on Nasdaq in 1995 and rolled up hundreds of local dental dealers into a $13.6B distributor before retiring as CEO at the end of 2025.
why: A dentist is a single-site buyer with no purchasing department, so the cost of changing supplier is the cost of rebuilding an ordering habit. Schein bought the local dealers and kept their sales reps, then put its own practice-management software on the front desk so the ordering system and the supplier became the same thing.
obst: An FTC complaint in 2018 accused Schein, Patterson and Benco of conspiring to refuse discounts to dental buying groups, and a parallel class action by practices forced years of litigation; Schein spun off its animal-health arm as Covetrus in 2019 partly under that pressure.
turn: The 1995 Nasdaq IPO, which gave a family distributor listed paper to buy Sullivan Dental, Meer Dental and hundreds of smaller dealers instead of competing with them on price.
